scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Born from a log raft during a 13th-century exile, Mugo transforms a single large drum into a ritual compass where dancers embody the four cardinal directions.
This is Mugo. 13th century (Goryeo period).
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (I0CkA4esxCo)
Title card: Mugo · South Korea · 13th century (Goryeo period)

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mugo originated during the Goryeo period (918–1392), specifically during the reign of King Chungnyeol (1274–1308).
According to the Goryeosa, it was created by Lee Hon, a government official in exile in Yonghae, who built a drum from a log raft.
The dance was later adopted by the Joseon dynasty court and performed by gisaeng at various official events.
on_screen: Map: South Korea · East Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a court dance (jeongjae) for palace banquets and local government ceremonies, it is also practiced as part of the Seungjeonmu ritual dance.
It symbolizes cosmic harmony through its directional alignment.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by eight dancers around a central large drum.
Four main dancers (wonmu) strike the drum with sticks, while four assisting dancers (hyeopmu) circle them holding flower-shaped sticks.
Dancers move in circular patterns, their positions dictated by the cardinal directions and their corresponding colors.
Watch for Wonmu drum strike, Hyeopmu circling.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Eight dancers; four inner (wonmu) and four outer (hyeopmu) surrounding a central drum

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear jackets in four specific colors representing directions: black (north), red (south), blue (east), and white (west).
The setting is typically a formal stage or courtyard with the drum as the focal point.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Lee Hon (이혼) is credited as the creator of the dance during his exile in the 13th century.
The dance has historically varied by the number of drums used, resulting in two-drum, four-drum, and eight-drum versions.
Mugo is a subclass of Korean court dance (jeongjae) and is closely related to Seungjeonmu.
